title: The forest years

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bharata refuses the throne, and Rama's sandals sit on it. Your line was not mine. What did you give back? Today, the three in the forest settle in. Day forty-five.

Picture it. A prince who grew up with servants and elephants. A princess who wore silk. A brother who was a general. Now: a hut made of leaves and branches that Lakshmana built by hand, on a hill called Chitrakoot, beside a river. They wear bark cloth. They eat fruit and roots. They bathe in the river at dawn. Rama points out the trees and birds to Sita, the flowers on the hillside, the elephants coming down to drink. For years, this is the whole story. No battles. No palace. Just three people, a hut, and a forest. And the strange thing is, in the text, they're happy.
screen: `A HUT OF LEAVES.` → `BARK, FRUIT, A RIVER AT DAWN.` → `THEY'RE HAPPY.`

segments.voice: After Bharata's visit they move on, deeper south, into the great Dandaka forest. And there they meet the sages who live in the woods. The sage Atri and his wife Anasuya, a holy woman famous for her devotion, who welcomes Sita like a daughter and gives her gifts and advice. The sage Agastya, who gives Rama divine weapons. The text says they spent about ten years moving from one hermitage to another, learning, listening, living simply. Eventually they settle at a place called Panchavati, by the Godavari river. Today's word: vanaprastha. Vana means forest. Vanaprastha: the one who goes to the forest. It's one of the four stages of life in Hindu tradition. First, the student. Second, the householder: work, family, raising children. Third, vanaprastha: when your children have children, you step back, let go of the business of the world, and turn toward the inner life. Fourth, the renouncer, who lets go of everything. Traditionally, the forest stage comes late. Rama is too young for it; he's there by exile, not by age. But those years look a lot like it. Fewer things. Fewer roles. More attention. Here's what the story knows. When everything was taken away from them, what was left turned out to be enough. Maybe more than enough. Most of us are carrying a lot we'll never need. Today's practice, and today's line, is one syllable. Less.
screen: `INTO THE DANDAKA FOREST.` · `ATRI, ANASUYA, AGASTYA.` · `VANAPRASTHA — TO THE FOREST.` · `THE FOUR STAGES OF LIFE.` · then, large: `LESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: simplicity for two minutes. If you can, put your phone face down, or out of reach. Sit with nothing in your hands. Don't plan. Don't fix anything. Just notice what's here: your breath, the air on your skin, the sounds around you, like the river at Chitrakoot. For these two minutes, you need nothing else. See if that's true. The bell holds the time.
Vanaprastha. The forest-dweller: the third stage of life, when you step back from the world and turn inward.
Your line: less. Today, do without one thing you'd normally reach for, and see if you miss it. Day forty-five.

howItsDone: Hindu tradition describes four stages of life (student, householder, forest-dweller, renouncer); today some older Hindus take up a simpler, more devotional life in the spirit of vanaprastha, and Chitrakoot and Panchavati are pilgrimage places.

original.note: Sanskrit: one who goes out to the forest (vana), the third stage of life.

trapdoor: what you thought: exile is a punishment in the woods.
what it means: stripped of almost everything, they find what's left is enough. vanaprastha, the forest stage.
what a scholar hears: the four ashramas are laid out in the dharma texts; Rama's forest life resembles vanaprastha, but he enters it by exile, not by age.
